scenes.heading: Building HTTP Services & Middleware
scenes.narration: In the next minute, let's see how Go builds production HTTP services from one tiny interface and one composition pattern.

scenes.heading: The building blocks
items: ServeMux routes patterns, with methods and wildcards
Middleware wraps a handler to add behavior
scenes.narration: The whole design rests on http.Handler, a single-method interface: ServeHTTP takes a response writer and a request. Because it's one method, routers, handlers, and middleware all speak it and compose trivially. ServeMux maps URL patterns to handlers, and since Go one point twenty-two it supports methods and path wildcards. Middleware is a function that takes the next handler and returns a new one, layering cross-cutting behavior around it.

scenes.heading: A request through the stack
steps: Server accepts, runs each request in a goroutine
Recovery catches any panic as a 500
Auth injects the user into r.Context()
The business handler writes the response
scenes.narration: Picture middleware as security layers wrapping your handler. The server accepts a connection and runs each request in its own goroutine. The request passes inward through logging, which times it; recovery, which catches a panic and returns a five hundred instead of crashing; and auth, which injects the authenticated user into the request context. Finally the business handler runs, and some layers also inspect the response on the way back out.

scenes.heading: Middleware plus method routing
scenes.narration: Here Logging is middleware: it returns a HandlerFunc that records the start time, calls the next handler inward, then logs the method, path, and elapsed time. The mux uses Go one point twenty-two routing to match a GET on a path wildcard and reads the id with PathValue. Because both the mux and the handler satisfy http.Handler, wrapping the entire mux in Logging applies it uniformly to every route.

scenes.text: Set ReadTimeout, WriteTimeout, IdleTimeout, and ReadHeaderTimeout; on SIGTERM call srv.Shutdown(ctx) to drain in-flight requests.
scenes.narration: One caution: a naked server has no timeouts, so a single slow client can pin a connection. Set read, write, idle, and read-header timeouts to defend against slow-loris attacks. And on SIGTERM, call Shutdown with a bounded context to stop accepting new connections and let in-flight requests finish, giving you safe, zero-downtime deploys.
